comparison: Both evaluate the generation of knockout mouse lines (C43, C50-C53) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides more detail about validation methods (immunofluorescence, western blot, mass spectrometry for C64-C65, C68), while peer reviewers accept the CRISPR/Cas9 methodology without critique.

Perfect agreement on fertility findings (C6-C9, C54-C56). Both evaluate as SUPPORTED and emphasize the dose-dependent phenotype with Cylc2 loss being less tolerated than Cylc1 loss. Both accept the inference that two functional alleles are required.

Both evaluate spatiotemporal localization (C59-C63) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of stage-specific imaging, while peer reviewers accept the dynamic localization pattern from acrosomal region to calyx without critique.

Both evaluate sperm count reductions (C71-C74) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval also addresses testicular morphology (C69-C70), while peer reviewer R4 focuses specifically on the dose-dependent sperm count findings.

OpenEval R6 addresses testicular morphology (C69-C70) as part of broader phenotyping. Peer R18 specifically affirms these findings, noting 'spermatogenesis appeared undisturbed' with normal germ cell types detected.

Both evaluate morphological defects (C77-C81) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of multiple imaging modalities, while peer reviewers affirm structural anomalies including acrosome attachment and head shape defects.

Both evaluate nuclear morphology and head shape findings (C82-C84) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative analysis and the inference that Cylc2 is the critical determinant, while peer reviewers accept the 'rounder and shorter' head phenotype.

Both evaluate calyx protein mislocalization (C85-C90) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval includes the inference connecting calyx disruption to morphological defects (C91), while peer reviewers accept the findings as part of comprehensive phenotyping.

OpenEval R9 addresses calyx formation defects including C91 (inference about calyx disruption causing morphology defects). Peer R3 explicitly affirms calyx formation defects (C10, C45, C91, C94-C95), stating Cylicins are 'essential for sperm calyx formation.'

OpenEval R10 evaluates ultrastructural PT defects (C92-C97) as SUPPORTED with TEM evidence. Peer R3 addresses overlapping calyx formation claims (C94-C95), affirming that 'calyx not forming in the absence of Cylicins.'

OpenEval R10 addresses ultrastructural defects including cytoplasm retention (C93). Peer R5 accepts 'impaired shedding of excess cytoplasm' (C12, C93, C115) as part of comprehensive structural defect phenotyping.

OpenEval R10 evaluates ultrastructural PT defects (C92-C97) with TEM. Peer R6 addresses overlapping structural defects (C92, C96) as part of broader morphological anomalies affecting head and head-neck region.

Both evaluate motility defects (C98-C102) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes dose-dependent effects and non-progressive circular swimming, while peer reviewers affirm 'decreased sperm motility' with similar defects in mouse and human.

OpenEval R12 evaluates flagellar beat analysis (C103-C106) as SUPPORTED, ruling out axonemal defects. Peer R7 addresses overlapping motility claims (C103-C104) as part of broader motility defect acceptance.

Both evaluate acrosome defects (C108-C113) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes stage-specific emergence during cap phase and temporal correlation with Cylicin localization. Peer reviewers affirm findings are 'in line with observations made in mice.'
OpenEval R15 addresses developmental defects including cytoplasm retention (C115). Peer R5 accepts 'impaired shedding of excess cytoplasm' as part of structural defects without specific critique.

Both evaluate manchette defects (C119-C125) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides quantitative measurements and notes dose-dependent effects. Peer reviewers affirm that 'manchette...persists in mature sperm of mice missing Cylc2.'

Both evaluate evolutionary analysis (C127-C132) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes CodeML analysis and preferential conservation of lysine residues. Peer reviewers affirm the 'interesting point' that higher conservation of Cylc2 explains more severe phenotype.

Both evaluate patient identification and genetic findings (C134-C146) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed variant characterization and VUS classification. Peer reviewers affirm the identification as 'interesting' with similar defects to mouse models.

Both evaluate patient phenotype (C147-C152) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes multiple levels of analysis (clinical, microscopic, immunofluorescence) and headless sperm phenotype. Peer reviewers affirm absence of CYLC1 protein provides evidence for essential role.

Both evaluate conserved calyx disruption (C153-C156) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes parallel phenotypes across species. Peer reviewers affirm 'findings from mouse models might be applicable to understanding human male infertility.'

OpenEval R22 evaluates functional conservation claims (C185-C187) as SUPPORTED, emphasizing parallel phenotypes and absence of CYLC1 protein. Peer R17 evaluates overlapping claims (C145, C185-C186, C192) as UNCERTAIN due to CYLC2 variant not being identified as pathogenic.

OpenEval R23 evaluates population genetics data (C189-C193) as SUPPORTED but notes unresolved discrepancy between mouse and human constraint data. Peer R17 evaluates overlapping claim C192 as UNCERTAIN, questioning CYLC2 variant pathogenicity.

Both evaluate mechanistic hypotheses (C170, C173, C177-C178) similarly. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting they are 'explicitly stated as hypotheses' lacking direct experimental evidence. Peer reviewers accept as SUPPORTED but note study is 'rather descriptive without molecular mechanism studies.'
OpenEval evaluates qRT-PCR data showing 50% Cylc2 reduction in heterozygotes (C57-C58) as SUPPORTED, ruling out transcriptional compensation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluates molecular weight discrepancies (C66-C67) as UNCERTAIN due to unexplained ~30 kDa difference between observed and predicted sizes. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluates the inference connecting mouse phenotype to human OAT syndrome (C107) as SUPPORTED based on oligozoospermia, asthenozoospermia, and teratozoospermia. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluates hypotheses about partial redundancy and dosage requirements (C179-C182) as SUPPORTED, integrating evolutionary and functional data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
